paras: The attempted lynching of Gus Harris and Loomis Wilson was a reported rush on the jail at Vandalia, Michigan, in early May 1888 by a crowd of Black residents seeking two Black men held on suspicion of murdering John Atkens. According to a wire dispatch, the unarmed crowd could not get into the jail, and no one was hurt. The story ran under lynching headlines as far as Washington and Dakota, though fuller regional accounts of the murder do not mention an attack on the jail.

John Aikens, a 28-year-old Black man of Calvin township in Cass County, disappeared on December 23, 1887, after drinking at a shooting match and then at the house of Gus Harris. The Telegram-Herald described the township as "largely inhabited by colored people" and said Aikens was popular in the Long Lake region. A young Black man, Lewis Wilson, later said that Harris had killed Aikens and that the two of them had put the body in Shave Head Lake. Harris was arrested on suspicion, and Wilson, held by officers, escaped on a Wednesday and was recaptured.
On the Sunday before the body was found, more than 1,500 people gathered at the lake while divers searched for it.

Two fishermen found the body in the lake near the house of Alexander Aikens about May 4, and an inquest was begun there. The body bore marks of a heavy blow on the neck and another behind the ear, and the forehead was crushed. An Elkhart dispatch placed the discovery in Long lake and said the neck was broken.

A wire dispatch from Vandalia said that when the news spread, about 1,500 "colored people of both sexes" rushed the jail, but being unarmed could not get in. The dispatch added that Harris and Wilson "would have been lynched" had the crowd reached them. It said Wilson made a partial confession after the crowd dispersed, that further arrests were expected, and that trouble was "looked for to night."

No report of further trouble at the jail appears in the coverage. By early June, Wilson had been held for trial at Cassopolis on a charge of murdering a man named "Akin." Gus Harris, a Dr. Harris and Charles Copley, all of whom Wilson had accused, were discharged. No report of a verdict at the inquest or of a trial was found.

The jail story reached readers through a single Chicago wire, which the Alexandria Gazette and the Washington Evening Star printed on May 5. The Evening Star headed it "Lymphers [Lynchers] After Two Murderers," and the Wheeling Sunday Register ran a shortened version the next day as "A Lynching Bee." On May 10 the Jamestown Weekly Alert in Dakota printed it under "Would Lynch Them. Negroes of Vandalia, Mich., Excited Over a Murder," with a deck saying the crowd meant to ornament "Lamp Posts With Carcasses."

Papers nearer the scene told the story differently. The Michigan Telegram-Herald ran it as "A Murder Mystery" among state news, with details of the disappearance, the inquest and Wilson's account, but said nothing of a mob. The Indianapolis Journal's Elkhart dispatch also omitted any mob and said Wilson's confession was "supposed to have been made for the purpose of diverting the suspicion" from himself.

Copies of the wire disagree on the size of the crowd: about 1,500 in the Alexandria, Wheeling and Jamestown printings, and "one hundred and fifty" in the Evening Star. The only other 1,500 figure in the coverage is the Telegram-Herald's count of people at the lake during the diving, and neither independent account mentions a rush on the jail, so the attack rests on the wire alone. The accounts also differ on timing: the wire puts Wilson's partial confession after the crowd dispersed, while the Michigan and Elkhart reports say he had told his story before the body was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Gus Harris and Loomis Wilson
bases: A wire report said a large crowd rushed the jail holding two murder suspects and would have lynched them had it got in (A1, A2, A6); no one was killed.

No one was killed; the wire describes an unarmed crowd of 150 or 1,500 that failed to enter the jail and would have lynched the two accused men (A1, A2), an attempt reported in the wire version only and absent from the fuller Michigan account (A3).

The rush on the jail appears only in one wire dispatch reprinted by several papers (A1, A2, A5, A6); the Michigan and Elkhart accounts of the same day describe the body's discovery but no attack on the jail (A3, A4).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: When news of the body spread, a crowd of colored people rushed the jail but, unarmed, could not get in; Harris and Wilson would have been lynched had the crowd reached them; Wilson confessed in part after the mob dispersed.

accounts.label: Michigan state-news account
accounts.gist: Wilson's story had been told before the body was found and was confirmed in part by its discovery; an inquest was begun; 1,500 people gathered at the lake the previous Sunday while divers searched; no attack on the jail is mentioned.

accounts.label: Elkhart dispatch
accounts.gist: The body was found in Long lake; Wilson's confession was suspected of being made to divert suspicion from himself; no mob is mentioned.

framing.detail: Eastern papers ran the Chicago wire under lynching headlines such as 'Lymphers [Lynchers] After Two Murderers' and 'A Lynching Bee', with no comment.
The Jamestown Weekly Alert headed it 'Would Lynch Them. Negroes of Vandalia, Mich., Excited Over a Murder', with a deck about 'Ornamenting Lamp Posts With Carcasses'.
The Michigan account treated the case as 'A Murder Mystery' and did not mention a mob.
